job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Diego Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Diego, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior test engineer at a switchgear factory in Halvorn. That's the big grey boxes that sit between a power line and a building. I started in September after an electrical engineering degree, and I did a six-week internship at a substation contractor. Each day I wire up a test rig, run a unit through its trip checks and write the results into a report. I share a flat above a bakery with my mate Tomas, and about a third of my pay goes to my student loan and rent. Football on Saturdays keeps me sane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me, though I'd say it with a shrug. At the plant we've already got software that writes up our test reports, so I'd say it's useful but not magic. To my mates I'd say it's overhyped, and that the real story is how little junior engineers get paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not sure the hype being wrong is good for me. I'd like AI to speed up my paperwork so I can do the interesting testing. If it doesn't, I'm stuck doing reports for the same low pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and I'd use the AI report tool a bit more, since it's already there and saves me an hour a day. I'd spend that hour learning the protection relay side, which is where the better pay is. I'd also keep going to the plant union meetings, because the contract negotiation is next spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty okay, honestly. A bit bored, a bit stretched on money, but not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does your money go in a normal month, and what's the weak spot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Where does the money go? Rent is 480 a month for my half, the loan is about 150, and then food and the train. I save maybe 40 on a good month, so a broken laptop would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the contract is the bigger worry. What would you ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm slowed down, I'd be one of the juniors on a temporary contract. The temporary contract bothers me more than any AI does, because one slow quarter and the juniors are the first to go. I'd want them made permanent after a year.

say: I'd shrug and say it's **useful but not magic**, since our report software already exists.
I'd tell mates the real story is how little **junior engineers** get paid.
think: I'd like AI to speed up the **paperwork** so I can do the testing.
If it doesn't, I'm stuck on **reports** for the same low pay.
do: Use the AI report tool more and spend the saved **hour** learning protection relays.
Keep going to **union** meetings before the spring contract talks.
Save **40** a month when I can.
feel: I feel **okay**, a bit bored and stretched, but not scared.
S0.quote: The temporary contract bothers me more than any AI does, because one slow quarter and the juniors are the first to go.
fieldNote: Diego's worry is **contract security** more than technology, which fits his union leanings.
He already uses the report software and sees it as a tool, not a threat.
Money is tight but steady, so he's uneasy rather than anxious.

steps.text: Use the AI report tool for test write-ups
Spend the saved hour studying protection relays
Attend plant union meetings before spring contract talks
Save 40 a month in a separate account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, and we should get ready for it instead of arguing about it. At work I'd say the unions should push for retraining paid on company time. Online I'd say the winners shouldn't be only the firms that own the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, the report writing and test-plan drafting would go to software quickly. That's maybe half of my week. What stays is the physical rig work, because a person has to connect a 10,000-volt unit and trust what they see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the person at the plant who knows the AI test tools and the hardware. I'd sign up for the relay protection course that my manager Ilse offered. And I'd save a bit more, maybe 80 a month, by cutting my football subscription and my streaming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert, I guess. It's like the start of a match when you don't know if the other team is stronger. I want to play it, not watch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My colleague Piotr is 58 and writes test plans by hand, and he won't use the software, so he's the one the firm might not keep. I worry about him, because he's not close to retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about that worry yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with him for an hour a week and show him the tool. That's small, but it's what I can do. And I'd ask the union to bargain for what happens to people like him.

say: I'd say it's real and we should **get ready**, with retraining paid on company time.
Online I'd argue the gains shouldn't go **only** to firms that own the software.
think: Report writing and test-plan drafting, about **half** my week, would go to software fast.
The **rig work** stays, because someone must connect a 10,000-volt unit and trust it.
do: Become the plant's go-to person for **AI test tools** and hardware.
Sign up for the **relay protection** course my manager Ilse offered.
Cut football and streaming subscriptions to save **80** a month.
feel: I feel **alert**, like the start of a match against a stronger team.
S1.quote: My colleague Piotr is 58 and writes test plans by hand, and he won't use the software, so he's the one the firm might not keep.
fieldNote: Diego's first instinct is **practical learning** and helping colleagues, with collective bargaining as backup.
He rates his job as half-exposed and separates desk tasks from rig work clearly.
His concern for an older colleague shows solidarity beyond his own interests.

steps.text: Learn the AI test-plan tool well enough to teach colleagues
Enrol on the relay protection course Ilse offered
Cut football and streaming fees and save 80 a month
Ask the union to bargain for older colleagues' retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is mad. I'd say publicly that this needs an emergency plan from governments, and that firms shouldn't cut anyone until there's one. At work I'd stay calm for the team, but I'd talk to the union about a freeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my desk half disappears fast, and then my rig half is next in 2031. A factory with robots doing the wiring doesn't need me. I'm 22 and I'd have a loan and nothing to show for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put every spare coin into a cash cushion and tell Tomas that we need to keep the flat cheap. I'd ask my parents what they could manage, which isn't much, they run a small shop. I'd also apply for any maintenance technician or utility job, since people fixing machines might last longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like a drop in a lift. But I'd also be angry that the decision gets made in a boardroom miles from here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents, and what would you keep to yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would I tell my parents? That I'm fine and I'm making a plan, and then I'd go outside and kick a wall. They sacrificed to send me to university, and it would feel like I wasted it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the gap before robots arrive. How would you use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The one thing that gives me hope is the 3 years between thinking AI and the robots. That's three years of hands-on work that stays. I'd try to be the person who repairs and commissions the robots.

say: I'd call for an **emergency plan** and ask firms not to cut anyone until there is one.
At work I'd stay calm for the team and talk to the **union** about a freeze.
think: My desk half disappears fast, and my **rig half** is next around 2031.
I'd have a **loan** and nothing to show for the degree.
do: Put every spare coin into a **cash cushion** and keep the flat cheap.
Apply for **maintenance** and utility technician jobs, since fixing machines may last longer.
Ask my parents what they could manage, knowing it's **little**.
feel: I feel **sick**, like a drop in a lift, and angry the decision sits in boardrooms.
S2.quote: I'd try to be the person who repairs and commissions the robots.
fieldNote: Diego jumps quickly from fear to a **concrete angle**: repair and commissioning work during the three-year gap.
He hides his fear from his parents, who sacrificed for his degree.
Anger is aimed at boardrooms, consistent with his left-leaning, union-minded view.

steps.text: Put every spare coin into a cash cushion
Apply for maintenance and commissioning technician jobs at utilities
Ask the union to demand a layoff freeze
Ask my parents what rent help they can manage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do something sensible if we start now. I'd call on firms and governments to set up retraining funds, and I'd say it loudly at the union meeting. It's not a crisis if people use the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years feels like a long slow countdown. I'd have a few years of real pay to pay off the loan, and then the desk jobs are gone. My plan is to be too useful to the hardware side to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the relay protection course and then the commissioning course. I'd move money into paying the loan off faster, aiming to clear it by 2030. I'd also keep trying AI tools every month, so I know their weak points.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than two years. Five years feels like a long road with a cliff somewhere, but at least I can see the signs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk with five years that you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The risk is that firms use the five years to hire fewer people and leave the juniors to compete for what remains. I'd see my friends at software firms get laid off first, and that would shake me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if friends lost jobs first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my friends lost jobs, I'd offer them my sofa and help with applications. Not much, but you do it. And I'd stay close to the union so that someone argues for the juniors.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** to do something sensible if we start now.
I'd call for retraining **funds** and say so loudly at the union meeting.
think: Five years feels like a slow **countdown**, with a few years to clear my loan.
My plan is to become **too useful** on the hardware side to cut.
do: Take the relay protection course, then the **commissioning** course.
Pay the loan down faster, aiming to clear it by **2030**.
Try a new **AI tool** every month to learn its weak points.
feel: I feel **steadier** than with two years, like a road with a cliff but visible signs.
S3.quote: Five years feels like a long road with a cliff somewhere, but at least I can see the signs.
fieldNote: Diego uses time for **skills and debt**, with a target date, which shows planning more than worry.
He expects software friends to be hit first and would offer them practical help.
His mood stays anxious because the loan outlasts the safe years.

steps.text: Complete the relay protection course then the commissioning course
Pay the student loan down to clear it by 2030
Try a new AI tool each month and note its flaws
Stay active in the union so juniors have a voice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is time. I'd tell people that this is the moment to build retraining and income support, quietly and properly. It's not a drama, it's a project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years means I'd be 32 and could have a proper career in power systems before it bites. I'd still want a plan B, but I wouldn't feel the knife at my neck. I'd even look forward to the robots in a factory if they take the dull wiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the protection and commissioning courses and aim for a senior test role by 28. I'd save for a flat deposit, since renting forever sounds like a trap. And I'd keep a small fund of 3 months' pay as the safety cushion I don't have now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, with a bit of curiosity. If I'm honest, a bit excited too, because I'm the kind of person who likes new tools once they've been proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What worries me is the wage side. Even if the jobs exist, will they pay properly? I'd want a union contract that shares productivity gains, not just a nice job title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your dad wants you to start your own business. Do you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad says I should go into business for myself in ten years. Maybe I'll start a small testing and repair outfit, where machines need a human who signs the certificate.

say: I'd say this is a **project**, not a drama, and we should build retraining and income support properly.
I'd say it **quietly**, to anyone who'll listen.
think: At 32 I could have a proper **power systems** career before the change bites.
I'd even welcome **robots** if they take the dull wiring.
do: Finish the protection and commissioning courses and aim for a **senior test role** by 28.
Save for a flat **deposit** instead of renting forever.
Build a **three-month** pay cushion I don't have now.
feel: I feel **calm**, with curiosity and a little excitement.
S4.quote: I'd want a union contract that shares productivity gains, not just a nice job title.
fieldNote: With ten years Diego plans a **career ladder** and talks about owning a certificate-signing business.
His remaining worry is pay and sharing gains, not whether work exists.
He remains uneasy because debt and a thin cushion don't vanish in a decade of change.

steps.text: Finish protection and commissioning courses by 26
Build a three-month cash cushion first
Save a flat deposit over the next six years
Push the union for a contract that shares productivity gains

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, for sure. I don't have the cushion or the time to move. What would help is a paid retraining scheme, a rule that juniors get permanent contracts, and the union at the table when the plant decides how to use AI.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people my age aren't scared of technology. We're scared of being the ones who pay for someone else's decision. Give us a fair seat, and we'll do the learning.

headlineQuote: People my age aren't scared of technology. We're scared of being the ones who pay for someone else's decision.
portrait: Diego is a **junior test engineer** at a switchgear factory, in a shared flat, with a heavy student loan.
He's **open to change** once it's proven, already uses AI report tools, and learns practical skills like protection relays.
He leans on the **union** and speaks up for older colleagues and temporary-contract juniors.
His mood rises with time: **alarm** at two years, steadier at ten.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because his loan, thin cushion and lack of family help leave no room.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **retraining**, permanent contracts for juniors, and a union seat when the plant decides how to use AI.
